newsitem.title: USA: Sweden helped Nazi war effort -- document says.
newsitem.headline: Sweden helped Nazi war effort -- document says.

text.p: Swedish collaboration with Nazi Germany included making parts for Hitler's deadly V-2 rockets, according to a Second World War document released on Friday by the World Jewish Congress.

Shifting its research focus to Sweden after a bruising battle with Switzerland over its wartime actions, the WJC released a letter in which a New York port offical told the U.S. Secretary of State that an American ship had discovered V-2 rocket parts that said "Made in Sweden."

The WJC also released a previously secret U.S. intelligence document quoting "reliable sources" as saying that some Swedish Red Cross representatives carried illegal correspondence between Nazis in Germany to sympathisers in Sweden after the war.

The 1946 document said the letters were carried "at a price" and that the representatives carried out cheaply purchased silverware, paintings and art objects from war-ravaged Germany for resale at higher prices in Sweden.

The V-2 rocket document, a letter from a New York port official to Secretary of State Edward Stettinius, said that the S.S. William Dean Howells had come under V-2 rocket attack while visiting the newly liberated port of Antwerp, Beligum, in January 1945.

The crew recovered "finely machined gears and shafts" that carried the clear imprint "Made in Sweden", and the official asked that the U.S. government protest strongly to Sweden that as a neutral country it could not make war weapons "which are delivered to the enemy in order to kill our Allies and our own people."
V-2 rockets were responsible for killing thousands of people during the war.

The WJC has spent more than a year combing the U.S. National Archives to trace Switzerland's relationship with Nazi Germany, uncovering many documents that described close Swiss bank collaboration with the Reichsbank.
The investigation into the archives began as an effort to trace the assets of Holocaust victims.

On Wednesday three of Switzerland's biggest banks set up a $70 million Holocaust memorial fund, and a WJC spokesman said the organisation would now shift its focus to the actions of other neutral countries during the war.
"There is a shift (in research) due to changing political circumstances in which the relationship with Switzerland is now marked by cooperation, not confrontation," the spokesman said.
